description: Width tiers for Year 8 Science — ACARA v9. Covers the seven U-strand descriptors only. H-strand (AC9S7H01–H04) and I-strand (AC9S7I01–I08) are banded with Year 7 and are covered in science_y7_width_tiers.json.
subject: Science

width_notes.minimum_width: The narrowest honest floor for the descriptor's command term — the fewest phenomena or contexts that still genuinely satisfy what the descriptor requires. For all Y8 U-strand descriptors, minimum is the command term met in one named context or with one named system, not a survey of all elaboration examples.
width_notes.typical_width: The full scope of the descriptor as ACARA intended it, grounded in the most common elaboration cases. Covers the range of content the descriptor addresses — biological, geological, physical or chemical — without requiring every elaboration to be used.
width_notes.wider: Enrichment directions that add phenomena, cultural contexts, historical cases or real-world applications — not harder versions of the same context. First Nations directions are included as default wider directions where elaborations indicate them. Cross-strand connections to H-strand descriptors are flagged where they provide substantive enrichment.
width_notes.elaborations: ACARA elaborations are treated as source data for the intended range of contexts and phenomena. Typical width is grounded in the most common elaboration cases; wider may infer beyond elaborations where clearly within the descriptor's territory and year band.

AC9S8U01.minimum_width: Identify and state the function of at least five organelles in plant and/or animal cells, correctly distinguishing which are present in each cell type; describe how the microscope enabled discovery of cell structures not visible to the naked eye.
AC9S8U01.typical_width: Describe the structure and function of all major organelles across plant and animal cells; explain how the function of each organelle contributes to what the cell can do; trace how successive improvements in microscopy revealed finer cell structures and contributed to cell theory; design or evaluate a physical or digital model of a cell.
wider: Investigate specialist cell types (red blood cells, nerve cells, guard cells, root hair cells) and explain how each cell's organelle complement reflects its specific function
Examine prokaryotic cells and compare their structure with eukaryotic cells — exploring what the absence of membrane-bound organelles means for cell function
Construct a timeline of microscopy developments and the cell discoveries each enabled — connecting technology development to knowledge change (AC9S8H01)
Explore how digital microscopes and contemporary imaging tools are used in current cell biology research
elaborations: exploring an augmented or virtual reality tour of a plant or animal to 'zoom in' and understand the scale of cells
identifying the structure and function of organelles in cells including the nucleus, cell membrane, cell wall, cytoplasm, chloroplasts and vacuoles
examining a variety of cells, including single-celled organisms, using a light microscope, a digital microscope, simulations and photomicrographs
comparing the similarities and differences of plant cells and animal cells visible with a light microscope and represented in a digital or physical model
designing a physical or digital model of a cell and explaining how the representation models the cell
considering how the invention of the microscope has contributed to understanding of cell structure

AC9S8U02.minimum_width: Describe the organisational hierarchy from cell to tissue to organ to organ system with examples from one named system; explain at least two structure-function relationships within that system.
AC9S8U02.typical_width: Analyse structure-function relationships across cell, tissue and organ levels in both a plant and an animal organ system; explain how each level of organisation contributes to the system's overall function; describe how the system enables survival of the organism; examine how a disorder at cell or tissue level affects organ function.
wider: Compare analogous plant and animal systems that achieve the same functional goal through different structural solutions (e.g. vascular transport in plants vs circulatory system in animals)
Investigate how an artificial organ mimics or augments the function of a real organ — identifying which structural features must be replicated and which limitations remain (AC9S8H01, H03)
Use 2D and 3D representations of organ systems to understand how organ position within the body affects function
Research how a disorder at the cellular or tissue level cascades to threaten individual survival through a specific case study
elaborations: comparing 2-dimensional and 3-dimensional representations of organ systems to understand how organs are positioned within the body
comparing the structure and function of analogous systems in a plant and an animal
examining the specialised cells and tissues involved in structure and function of particular organs in an organ system
describing the structure of each organ in a system and relating its function to the overall function of the system
researching how a disorder in cells or tissues can affect how an organ functions, such as how hardening of the arteries can lead to poor circulation or heart disease
investigating how an artificial organ mimics or augments the function or functions of a real organ

AC9S8U03.minimum_width: Describe the geological features produced at each of the three plate boundary types (divergent, convergent, transform); identify at least two lines of evidence supporting the theory of plate tectonics.
AC9S8U03.typical_width: Explain the geological features and plate movements at each boundary type, including sub-types of convergent boundaries; trace the development of evidence from continental drift to plate tectonics including Marie Tharp's contribution; describe how tectonic activity distributes earthquake and volcanic hazards; examine engineering and scientific responses that support communities near active boundaries.
wider: Construct a timeline of evidence for plate tectonics — examining why Wegener's continental drift hypothesis was initially rejected and what additional evidence was required for acceptance (AC9S8H01)
Research First Nations Australians' cultural accounts of earthquakes and volcanic events and explore how long-term observational records contribute to understanding of tectonic history
Investigate how the extreme age and stability of the Australian craton relates to its plate tectonic history — contrasting with active margins in the Asia-Pacific region
Explore how seismic data is shared between Asia-Pacific governments and used for tsunami early warning systems (AC9S8H04)
elaborations: examining patterns of earthquake and volcanic activity over time and proposing explanations
evaluating the impact of tectonic events on human populations and examining engineering solutions designed to reduce the impact
modelling interactions at plate boundaries
investigating the relative significance of different forces involved in tectonic plate movement including slab pull, ridge push and convection
relating the extreme age and stability of a large part of the Australian continent to its plate tectonic history
constructing a timeline of evidence to show the development of the theory of plate tectonics
exploring how geologist and oceanographic cartographer Marie Tharp's topographic maps of the Atlantic Ocean floor provided support for the acceptance of the theory of plate tectonics
researching First Nations Australians' cultural accounts that provide evidence of earthquakes and volcanoes

AC9S8U04.minimum_width: Name and describe at least four rock cycle processes; classify rock samples as sedimentary, igneous or metamorphic from observable properties; explain how the formation process of one rock type determines at least one of its properties.
AC9S8U04.typical_width: Describe the complete rock cycle including all major processes and the timescales involved; explain how formation conditions (temperature, pressure, cooling rate, sediment type) determine the observable properties of each rock type; explain how properties derived from formation determine the uses of specific rocks; use a dichotomous key to classify rock samples.
wider: Investigate the traditional geological knowledge of First Nations Australians used in selecting rock types for tools (grindstones, hammerstones, cutting tools) — examining deep empirical knowledge of rock properties
Examine fossil evidence (body, trace, opalised) to reconstruct the formation conditions of the sedimentary rock containing them
Research how mining of ores and minerals impacts local environments and examine environmental rehabilitation initiatives
Connect the rock cycle to plate tectonics — examining how tectonic forces drive rock cycle processes including uplift, subduction and volcanic activity (AC9S8U03)
elaborations: comparing the observable properties of different types of rocks and identifying them using a provided dichotomous key
exploring the major processes of the rock cycle including weathering, erosion, deposition, melting, crystallisation, uplift, heat and pressure in the formation of different types of rocks
analysing the role of forces and heat energy in the formation of different types of rocks and comparing how quickly or slowly different processes can occur
examining fossil evidence, such as body, trace or opalised fossils, to predict how and when a rock was formed
explaining the uses of different types of rocks with reference to their properties and formation
exploring the traditional geological knowledges of First Nations Australians that are used in the selection of different rock types for different purposes
investigating how First Nations Australians have used quarrying to access rocks for use as or production of everyday objects such as grindstones, hammerstones, anvils and cutting tools
exploring how the mining of ores and minerals impacts on local environments and examining environmental rehabilitation initiatives

AC9S8U05.minimum_width: Classify at least four energy types as kinetic or potential with examples; trace at least two energy transfers or transformations through a named simple system; identify heat as a by-product in at least one energy transfer.
AC9S8U05.typical_width: Classify the full range of energy types across both kinetic and potential categories; trace complete energy transfer and transformation sequences through simple systems (roller-coaster, Newton's cradle, electrical circuit) using labelled flow diagrams; distinguish transfers from transformations; explain why heat production as a by-product reduces the useful energy available from a transfer.
wider: Investigate traditional fire-starting methods used by First Nations Australians and identify all energy transformations involved — from mechanical kinetic energy through friction heat to combustion
Analyse a Rube Goldberg machine and identify all energy transfers and transformations in sequence — applying the framework to a complex multi-step system
Examine the development of hybrid, electric and hydrogen vehicles as engineering responses to energy dissipation and fossil fuel depletion (AC9S8H03)
Investigate how electrical circuit resistance affects heat production as a by-product — connecting energy dissipation to circuit design principles
elaborations: investigating relationships between kinetic and potential energy in a simple system such as a roller-coaster or Newton's cradle
classifying types of energy as either kinetic energy such as movement, heat and electricity or potential energy such as chemical, elastic and gravitational
critiquing and using representations such as flow diagrams to illustrate changes between different forms of energy in a system
identifying where heat energy is produced as a by-product of energy transfer, such as filament light globes, exercise, and battery charging and use
using electrical circuits and components to demonstrate electrical energy transfer and its transformation into heat, light and sound
observing a Rube Goldberg machine and identifying the energy transfers and transformations involved
investigating traditional fire-starting methods used by First Nations Australians and their understandings of the transformation of energy

AC9S8U06.minimum_width: Classify at least five substances as elements, compounds or mixtures with atomic/molecular reasoning; identify at least eight elements by chemical symbol; write or interpret formulas for at least three simple compounds.
AC9S8U06.typical_width: Explain the element/compound/mixture classification hierarchy using particle-level reasoning; distinguish mixture sub-types (solutions, suspensions, colloids); use element symbols and molecular formulas to represent and interpret substances; compare 2D and 3D representations of matter and identify the strengths and limitations of each.
wider: Examine how Mendeleev arranged elements in the first periodic table and compare with the current version — tracing how knowledge of atomic structure refined the classification system (AC9S8H01)
Create a timeline showing how the concept of an element has changed from Democritus through Dalton to the modern atomic model
Compare different representation types for the same substance — symbol, formula, 2D diagram, 3D ball-and-stick model — and explain what each adds and what each omits
Investigate how mixture composition is represented and managed in industrial contexts — alloy specifications, solution concentrations, ore grades in mining
elaborations: using virtual and physical models to distinguish between elements and compounds in terms of types of atoms
examining how Dmitri Mendeleev arranged the elements in the first version of the periodic table and comparing his arrangement with the current version
explaining why elements are represented by symbols, compounds and molecules by formulas and mixtures by percentages
using representations to show the classification of matter as elements, compounds and different types of mixtures such as solutions, suspensions and colloids
examining the information conveyed by different types of representations of elements and compounds and identifying where and why these different representations are used
creating a timeline or models to show how the concept of an element has changed over time from Democritus to John Dalton

AC9S8U07.minimum_width: Classify at least three changes as physical or chemical with justification; identify at least three observable indicators of chemical change; classify a named reaction as exothermic or endothermic based on temperature change evidence.
AC9S8U07.typical_width: Explain the fundamental physical/chemical change distinction using particle-level reasoning; identify and use observable indicators (gas production, precipitate, colour change, temperature change) as evidence for chemical reactions; perform or analyse simple reactions to identify indicators; distinguish exothermic from endothermic reactions using temperature data; interpret data on substance properties before and after interaction to determine change type.
wider: Investigate how chemical change indicators are used in diagnostic testing contexts — soil kits, water quality tests, medical testing — examining how the same observable indicators are applied purposefully
Examine everyday processes that challenge student intuitions about the physical/chemical distinction — dissolving, cooking, rusting, digestion — and use particle-level reasoning to classify each
Investigate traditional fire-starting methods used by First Nations Australians — examining the chemical reactions and energy transformations involved (AC9S8U05)
Research how the physical and chemical properties of a substance affect its production or use — connecting the change distinction to materials selection in engineering
elaborations: performing simple chemical reactions to identify the indicators of chemical change such as gas production, solid production, colour change and temperature change
analysing and interpreting data on the properties of substances before and after the substances interact to determine if a chemical or physical change has occurred
investigating and identifying energy changes in different chemical reactions such as differences in temperature
examining how the physical and chemical properties of a substance will affect its production or use
discussing where indicators of chemical change are used for identifying the presence of particular substances, such as in soil, water and medical testing kits
